title: Community Incarnates Classical Education
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: John Mark Reynolds argues that classical education needs a living community, not just a canon, to keep students rooted and keep them from coming unmoored. He starts with his great-grandfather's Bible, which ties him to a family and shows how physical objects and inherited customs carry meaning for souls with bodies. He says schools were once places that gave generations a shared culture, but mobility and the pursuit of diplomas have weakened those ties. A canon read across generations helps, yet classically educated thinkers have sometimes used their learning to isolate themselves from the surrounding town, so he calls for a virtuous school community that strengthens bonds to family, church and neighbors. He sketches its marks: loving a place, honoring persons over stuff, rarely changing customs, depending on Christ, and keeping some whimsy that exposes educational flimflam. He closes by recommending traditions such as a signing book or name wall so graduates feel part of something greater than an isolated self.
points: A classical school needs a living community of customs, place and people, because a canon alone does not keep students from becoming unmoored.
Classical learning can isolate scholars from the surrounding town, so a virtuous school community should deliberately strengthen ties to family, church and neighbors.
Schools should love their place, open their campuses appropriately to the town, and treat members as the reason for the community rather than as means.
Customs should be changed rarely so generations recognize the school, joined to older classical schools so even a new school feels old.
Whimsy and laughter, along with rituals such as signing a book or marking names on a wall, protect a school from fashionable consultants and root graduates in the alma mater.
quotes: Skills must be acquired, and diplomas are practical, but “to know self” and see God requires stronger stuff. A school is not a fundamental social category. We need families and the church.

Without a strong community grounded in the past and serving the area, consistent with the values of family, church, we can get lost. We come unmoored. Canonical education naturally helps with this problem.
Sometimes we even boast of the separation of “town and gown”. Townies are stereotyped as servants at best and barbarians at worst. “Gownies” are sneered at as useless parasites on the community.
A virtuous community is one that enables members to flourish and strengthens virtuous ties to family, church, and the broader community.
A community exists to help humans flourish, not books in libraries, buildings, or any other stuff.
The school that laughs at itself will not easily fall for “consultants” or other flimflam men who so infect education.

Celebrate the alma mater, and the graduates will be celebrated as members of that community. Make sure that, from the very start of a college or school, there is a book they can sign or a wall where names are placed as each generation of teachers and graduates come and go.
